docs.title: quantumHams
docs.text:
quantumHams provides backend-neutral Hamiltonian models for quantum-computing technologies, with a portable SciPy implementation and optional CUDA-Q integration.

Start with the usage guide or learn how to add a new technology.

docs.title: Extending quantumHams
docs.text:
1. Create a technology-specific package under src/quantumhams/.
  2. Implement a class derived from HamiltonianModel.
  3. Expose n_qubits and pauli_hamiltonian().
  4. Represent the physics using PauliTerm objects.
  5. Add analytical unit tests for small systems and numerical tests for invariants.
  6. Export the stable public class from quantumhams.__init__.

Backends consume only PauliHamiltonian, so a new physical model does not need backend-specific code. A new backend implements the SimulationBackend protocol and is registered in backends/registry.py.

docs.title: Rubidium neutral atoms
docs.text:
The implemented effective two-level model is

[H = \frac{\Omega}{2}\sum_i X_i - \sum_i \Delta_i n_i + \sum_{i<j}\frac{C_6}{r_{ij}^6}n_i n_j.]

All numerical parameters must use a mutually consistent unit system. quantumHams intentionally does not silently convert angular frequency, frequency, distance, or interaction units.

docs.title: Ytterbium trapped ions
docs.text:
The initial trapped-ion model is an effective long-range Ising/Mølmer–Sørensen Hamiltonian:

[H = \sum_{i<j} J_{ij}X_iX_j + \sum_i B_i Z_i.]

Use an explicit coupling matrix or construct a distance-dependent power-law approximation.

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text: HamiltonianModel.evolve() accepts a bit string, basis-state integer, or normalized state vector and an ordered sequence of non-negative sample times.

docs.title: Native CUDA-Q Dynamics evolution
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from quantumhams import NeutralAtomRegister, RubidiumRydbergHamiltonian

model = RubidiumRydbergHamiltonian(
    atom_register=NeutralAtomRegister.linear(2, 5.5),
    rabi_frequency=2 * np.pi,
    detuning=0.0,
    c6=2 * np.pi * 862_690.0,
)

# Requires CUDA-Q and a supported CUDA runtime. No SciPy delegation occurs.
result = model.evolve("00", np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 101), backend="cudaq")
print(result.backend)       # cudaq
print(result.states.shape)  # (101, 4)

# Default: try CUDA-Q, then safely fall back to SciPy if runtime execution fails.
portable_result = model.evolve("00", np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 101))
print(portable_result.backend)  # cudaq or scipy
